attributes.body:
Although のに is often thought of as a simple combination of the particles の and に, it is actually its own particle, with the meaning of 'despite', or 'in order to'. In this lesson, we will focus primarily on the 'despite' nuance.

Due to のに being a conjunction particle, it can be linked to almost any word type, to show that 'despite (A), (B)'. As with many conjunction particles, な will be required after a noun/な-Adjective, but before のに.

It is also possible to see だのに, instead of なのに, but this is something that is only seen in certain dialects, and would be considered incorrect by the vast majority of native speakers.

Fun Fact

Regardless of having two quite different translations ('despite', and 'in order to'), のに always functions in the same way.

In the situation of '(A) のに, (B)', (B) is/will be the result.

The only difference between how the nuance will be read, is whether the (B) statement is a logical conclusion, or an illogical one. When logical, the meaning is usually 'in order to', when 'illogical', the meaning is usually 'despite'.

attributes.source: [DBJG] A Dictionary of Basic Japanese Grammar

attributes.body: ものを and のに both are used to express the sense of 'if only'. ものを is more formal and also typically used when the speaker is expressing their disappointment at something that should have happened, not happening, e.g. 事前に知らせてくれればいいものを ('if only you had informed me in advance'), while のに can be used for general wishes 晴れればいいのに ('if only the weather were nice').

first_relatable.title: ものを
first_relatable.meaning: But, Although, If only, I wish I had

attributes.body: Both のに and くせに express contrast, but with different nuance. のに is relatively neutral, like 'although', while くせに adds a strong negative or critical tone. For example, 頭がいいのにやる気がない and 頭がいいくせにやる気がない both mean 'Although (he's) smart, (he) has no motivation.', the のに version is just stating a fact, while the くせに version implies that his lack of motivation is a negative trait and not befitting of him.

のに expresses contrast, similar to 'although,' and follows verbs, adjectives, or nouns (with な for nouns and な-adjectives). It's typically used at the end of a clause or sentence. それでも also shows contrast, but appears at the beginning of a sentence. The それ refers to the previous statement, giving it the meaning of 'Even so' or 'But still.'

first_relatable.title: それでも
first_relatable.meaning: But still, And yet, Even so, Nevertheless

attributes.body: Both にしても and のに express contrast, but with different nuances. のに is a general contrastive expression, like 'although.' にしても often presents a hypothetical or assumed condition, followed by an unexpected result. Like other ～ても forms, it's commonly used with Wh-words, e.g. どこに行くにしても 'no matter where you go'.

first_relatable.title: にしても
first_relatable.meaning: Even though, Even if, Even when, Also

attributes.body: のに and ものの both express contrast, but differ in nuance and tone. のに is more casual and often conveys disappointment or regret. It can also end a sentence to imply 'If only (A)!'. ものの is more formal and means 'although (A), (B) didn't follow as expected,' often with an implicit contrast. Unlike のに, it is not generally used alone at the end of a sentence..

のに expresses contrast, similar to 'although,' and follows verbs, adjectives, or nouns (with な for nouns and な-adjectives). It's typically used at the end of a phrase or sentence. それなのに is a related form used at the beginning of a sentence, meaning 'and yet' or 'despite that,' with それ referring back to the previous statement.

Both のに and ながらも express contrast, but with different focuses. のに is more general and used widely, like the English 'although.' ながらも is mainly used with state-expressing verbs and conveys surprise that something happened despite that state.

second_relatable.title: ながらも
second_relatable.meaning: But, Even while, Even though, Despite, Although
